notes: The logo and the mark certificate are not downloaded, and DMARC enforcement, which BIMI requires, needs the BIMI check on a domain.

findings.explanation: Without DMARC, receivers apply their own handling to mail that fails SPF and DKIM alignment, and the domain owner receives no reports.
findings.message: No DMARC record was found for the domain or any of its parent domains.
findings.recommendation: Publish a DMARC record, for example with p=none and a rua address, and use the reports to plan further steps.

findings.explanation: The resolver answered NXDOMAIN: it found no records for this name. Another resolver or a recent registration or delegation change could give a different answer.
findings.message: The DNS resolver reported that the domain does not exist.
findings.recommendation: Check the spelling and that the domain is registered and delegated.

notes: The policy shown is the record's own p=; for a subdomain the sp= or np= value can apply instead. The DMARC check on a domain decides which record and policy apply.
Whether a report address in another domain accepts reports (RFC 9989 external destination verification) needs DNS and is not checked.

body_example.policy:
version: STSv1
mode: testing
mx: mx1.example.com
mx: *.mail.example.com
max_age: 604800

notes: Only the policy text is read. Whether the domain publishes an _mta-sts record, serves this file at https://mta-sts.<domain>/.well-known/mta-sts.txt and lists matching MX hosts needs the MTA-STS check.

findings.explanation: In testing mode senders report TLS failures through TLS-RPT but still deliver the mail, so the policy does not yet protect against downgrade attacks.
findings.message: The MTA-STS policy is in testing mode.
findings.recommendation: Move to mode enforce once TLS-RPT reports show that all MX hosts pass.

findings.explanation: The domain receives mail, but none of its MX host names matches a provider on Lookproof's fixed list. The domain may run its own mail servers or use a provider that is not on the list.
findings.message: The MX hosts match no provider on the list.

summary: Reverse DNS check for mail servers

notes: Each include and redirect is counted once here; the records they point to can need more DNS lookups. The SPF check on a domain counts the whole tree.

findings.explanation: ~all asks receivers to accept mail from servers that are not listed but treat it as suspicious. With an enforcing DMARC policy (p=quarantine or p=reject in effect; t=y counts one step lower) that is enough, because DMARC decides what happens to forged mail. Without one, receivers may still deliver it, and -all (fail) is the stronger ending.
findings.message: The SPF policy ends with softfail (~all).
findings.recommendation: If DMARC is not enforcing yet, confirm that every legitimate sender is listed and then end the record with a hard fail instead of softfail. With an enforcing DMARC policy, softfail is acceptable.

notes: This describes the domain's published policy, not whether forged mail gets through: the receiving server makes the final decision, and DKIM is not assessed.
Report addresses are not contacted; whether an https: endpoint accepts reports is not checked.

findings.explanation: A name server such as ns1.example.com for example.com can only be found through glue: address records the parent zone publishes with the delegation. Keep the glue at the registrar in step when the server's address changes.
findings.message: A name server lies inside the zone it serves and needs glue records.

findings.explanation: The name server's name matches no provider on Lookproof's fixed, versioned list. It can be the domain's own server, a registrar's or a smaller provider's, so this is information, not a problem. The evidence names the server.
findings.message: A name server matches none of the DNS providers on the list.

notes: Rows marked cache show how long the public resolver may still keep the record, not the TTL set in the zone: the configured TTL is normally at least that long. Exact TTLs come only from a DNSSEC-signed zone whose answers the resolver validated.

findings.explanation: Services ask for a TXT record with a fixed prefix and a token to prove that someone controlled the domain. A token shows that the service was set up once; it does not prove that the service is in use today. The evidence names the services.
findings.message: The domain publishes verification records for one or more services.

body_example.zone:
$TTL 3600
@       IN SOA  ns1.example.com. hostmaster.example.com. (
                2026102701 ; serial
                7200       ; refresh
                3600       ; retry
                1209600    ; expire
                3600 )     ; minimum
        IN NS   ns1
        IN NS   ns2.example.net.
        IN MX   10 mail
        IN A    192.0.2.10
ns1     IN A    192.0.2.53
mail    IN A    192.0.2.25
www     IN CNAME @
www     IN TXT  "site-verification=abc123"

notes: The zone is read as text only: nothing is looked up, and DNSSEC signatures are not verified.

findings.explanation: A name with a CNAME may hold no other data except DNSSEC records (RFC 1034 section 3.6.2, RFC 2181 section 10.1). Resolvers then answer inconsistently and many loaders refuse the zone. The evidence names the other types.
findings.message: A name has a CNAME and other records at the same time.
findings.recommendation: Keep either the CNAME or the other records for that name.

notes: A request is only what its owner asks for: the CA decides which names and key usages the certificate gets.
data.subject: CN=www.example.com

notes: Nothing is fetched: the chain, revocation and trust in the issuer are not checked.
data.subject: O=Example Ltd,CN=www.example.com

findings.explanation: The block holds an email address (emailAddress in a name, or an rfc822Name in the subject alternative names) or a name type that can identify a person, such as a user principal name. Lookproof never returns or stores those. The evidence lists which kinds were present; all other fields are shown.
findings.message: Email addresses and personal name types were left out of the result.

body_example.header: Set-Cookie: __Secure-session=3f9a1c7e5b2d; Domain=example.com; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax; Max-Age=86400

data.name: __Secure-session
notes: Only the pasted text is read; whether a site sends this header is not checked.

body_example.header: Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline' https://cdn.example.com; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'self'

notes: Only the pasted text is read; whether a site sends this header is not checked.

findings.explanation: The script-src directive (or default-src, when there is no script-src) allows 'unsafe-inline' without a nonce or hash, or allows 'unsafe-eval'. Injected inline scripts can then run, which removes most of the protection the policy gives against cross-site scripting.
findings.message: The Content Security Policy allows inline or eval'd scripts.
findings.recommendation: Move inline scripts to files or allow them with nonces or hashes, and drop 'unsafe-eval' once no code needs eval().

notes: Only the pasted text is read; whether a site sends this header is not checked.
hstspreload.org also needs the site to redirect http to https on the same host and to send the header on the registrable domain over HTTPS; that needs a live check.

findings.explanation: Catalogs such as the x402 Bazaar list an endpoint from its payment requirements: the description says what a buyer gets, and the output schema (outputSchema in a v1 option, the bazaar extension in v2) says what the response looks like. Agents choose between endpoints from these two fields, so an endpoint without them is listed poorly or not at all. The evidence names what is missing.
findings.message: The 402 lacks a description or an output schema for catalogs.
findings.recommendation: Give the route a description, and declare the output schema with the bazaar extension (v2) or outputSchema (v1) in the payment middleware's route config.

findings.explanation: Agents look for files on the same origin before they call or pay: /llms.txt (a short description for language models), /openapi.json (the API's operations), /.well-known/agent-card.json (an A2A agent card), /mcp.json (an MCP server listing) and /.well-known/x402 (the capability manifest). Each file was fetched once without following redirects. The evidence gives the path and whether it was missing or answered with something else, often an HTML page that a single-page app serves for every path.
findings.message: A discovery file is missing on the endpoint's origin.
findings.recommendation: Serve the files that fit the API on the endpoint's own origin, with the right content type and status 200, and return 404 for paths that do not exist.

findings.explanation: The address before the slash is not the first address of the network, as in 192.0.2.5/24. The network is 192.0.2.0/24; many configuration files reject the other form or read it as a single host.
findings.message: The network was given with host bits set.
findings.recommendation: Write the network with its first address, as shown in the result.

findings.explanation: The address is in a special-purpose block (IANA's IPv4 and IPv6 Special-Purpose Address Registries), for example private, loopback, link-local, shared address space or documentation. The scope and its RFC are in the result. Such an address cannot be reached from the public internet.
findings.message: The address is not globally routable.
